questions.evidence: Published texts are easier to collect than informal conversations
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Published texts are easier to collect than informal conversations” The difference concerns evidence availability.

questions.stem: What does a word’s inclusion not necessarily show?
options: Universal approval among speakers
Evidence of an established use
A decision by editors to describe it
Examples of recurring meanings
questions.evidence: does not imply that every speaker approves
questions.explanation: Evidence: “does not imply that every speaker approves” Inclusion records usage rather than unanimous endorsement.

questions.stem: What does “sense” mean in the last paragraph?
options: A distinct meaning of a word
A speaker’s physical perception
A dictionary’s publication date
The sound of a conversation
questions.evidence: where one sense ends and another begins
questions.explanation: Evidence: “where one sense ends and another begins” The discussion concerns boundaries between related meanings.

questions.stem: Why are examples useful in an entry?
options: They show how a meaning functions in context
They eliminate all editorial judgment
They prove that every speaker uses a word
They replace the need to collect evidence
questions.evidence: Examples help readers see how a word operates in context
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Examples help readers see how a word operates in context” Context illustrates a sense without claiming complete representativeness.

items.title: Paying attention to a soundscape
items.passage:
An environment contains more than isolated sounds. The combination of voices, machines, animals, and moving air creates what researchers call a soundscape. People may evaluate the same sound differently depending on what they are doing. Conversation can make a public square feel lively but distract someone trying to study beside it.
Measuring sound intensity is useful, yet it does not capture every aspect of an experience. A steady ventilation hum and an irregular series of sharp noises can have similar average intensity while attracting different amounts of attention. Timing, frequency, and the meaning assigned to a sound all influence its effect. A familiar bell may convey helpful information even when it is louder than background noise.
Designing a comfortable environment therefore involves more than reducing a single number. Planners can consider where activities occur, when noises arise, and whether users can choose quieter spaces. Asking users about their experience complements physical measurements. Together, these approaches reveal why an intervention that improves one location might be less helpful in another.

questions.stem: What does the passage emphasize about managing sound?
options: Context and user experience matter alongside intensity measurements
Reducing average sound intensity is the most reliable way to improve each location
Irregular noises should be replaced with steady sounds regardless of users’ activities
Public sound design should chiefly increase the availability of informative bells
questions.evidence: involves more than reducing a single number
questions.explanation: Evidence: “involves more than reducing a single number” The author combines physical measures with timing, meaning, and activity.

questions.stem: Which feature may differ between sounds with similar average intensity?
options: How much attention they attract
Whether they can be measured at all
Their guaranteed effect on all listeners
Whether they form part of an environment
questions.evidence: attracting different amounts of attention
questions.explanation: Evidence: “attracting different amounts of attention” Steady and irregular sounds can have similar averages but different attentional effects.

questions.stem: Why might conversation be welcome in one setting and disruptive in another?
options: The activities and expectations of listeners differ
Its physical intensity cannot change
Only squares contain voices
Study spaces do not have soundscapes
questions.evidence: depending on what they are doing
questions.explanation: Evidence: “depending on what they are doing” The same sound is evaluated through the listener’s activity.

questions.stem: What does “these approaches” in the final paragraph include?
options: User reports and physical sound measurements
Only the use of quieter ventilation
The removal of bells and voices
A comparison of two average intensity values
questions.evidence: Asking users about their experience complements physical measurements
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Asking users about their experience complements physical measurements” The two complementary evidence sources are named immediately before the phrase.

questions.stem: Why does the author use the example of a familiar bell?
options: To show that a louder sound can serve a useful purpose
To prove bells are quieter than background noise
To argue that intensity is impossible to measure
To recommend bells in every study room
questions.evidence: may convey helpful information
questions.explanation: Evidence: “may convey helpful information” Meaning can make a sound useful despite its volume.

items.title: When a model is useful
items.passage:
A model represents selected features of a system rather than reproducing every detail. A simple model of traffic might describe how many vehicles enter a junction each minute while ignoring differences among drivers. Whether this simplification is acceptable depends on the question being asked. Estimating average congestion may require less detail than investigating how a particular collision occurred.
Adding complexity does not automatically improve a model. More variables require additional measurements, and uncertain values can introduce uncertain predictions. A complicated model can also be difficult to inspect, making errors harder to detect. Researchers often begin with a simpler version and add detail when comparisons with observations reveal a specific need.
A useful model should therefore be evaluated against its purpose and evidence. Agreement with one set of observations is encouraging, but testing it on other conditions offers a stronger check. When a prediction fails, the mismatch may reveal an omitted process. Models help organize reasoning precisely because their assumptions and limitations can be examined rather than hidden.

questions.stem: What is the author’s main claim?
options: A model’s value depends on purpose, evidence, and inspectable assumptions
Detailed models provide stronger evidence because they include more variables
A model is useful mainly when its original observations closely match its assumptions
Failed predictions show that a model needs more measurements rather than a revised process
questions.evidence: evaluated against its purpose and evidence
questions.explanation: Evidence: “evaluated against its purpose and evidence” The passage presents selective representation as useful when its limits are assessed.

questions.stem: What disadvantage can extra variables introduce?
options: Greater uncertainty from additional measurements
A guarantee of simpler inspection
A complete removal of assumptions
Less need for observations
questions.evidence: uncertain values can introduce uncertain predictions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “uncertain values can introduce uncertain predictions” Additional inputs can carry uncertainty rather than automatically improving accuracy.

questions.stem: Which traffic question may demand more detail?
options: How a specific collision happened
The average number of vehicles waiting
The average flow through a junction
Whether congestion is broadly increasing
questions.evidence: investigating how a particular collision occurred
questions.explanation: Evidence: “investigating how a particular collision occurred” Explaining an individual event may require features that an aggregate model omits.

questions.stem: What does “omitted” mean here?
options: Left out
Directly measured
Made more accurate
Repeated unnecessarily
questions.evidence: an omitted process
questions.explanation: Evidence: “an omitted process” A failed prediction may indicate something missing from the representation.

questions.stem: Why test a model under other conditions?
options: To check whether its success extends beyond one observation set
To ensure it matches only its original data
To eliminate the need to state assumptions
To prove no simpler version could work
questions.evidence: testing it on other conditions offers a stronger check
questions.explanation: Evidence: “testing it on other conditions offers a stronger check” Broader testing probes usefulness beyond the initial agreement.

items.title: Preserving a performance
items.passage:
Preserving a musical performance differs from preserving a painting. A painting remains as a physical object, whereas a performance unfolds through actions in time. A recording captures sound, but it may not show gestures, interaction, or the audience's response. Written notation preserves another aspect, yet it cannot specify every choice made by a performer.
Archivists therefore combine materials rather than assume that one record is sufficient. Programmes identify participants and context, video can document movement, and interviews can explain decisions that are not obvious from a recording. Such accounts must still be interpreted carefully: memories change, and performers may describe intentions differently after an event.
Preservation can also include teaching the practice to new participants. This sustains skills that a recording alone cannot transmit fully, although each new performance will differ. The aim is not necessarily to freeze one version forever. It may be to keep enough evidence and knowledge for future people to understand how the performance was created and why it mattered.

questions.stem: What challenge does the passage describe?
options: No single record captures every aspect of a performance
Combining recordings produces a permanent version that future performers should reproduce
Interviews are the most reliable records because performers can explain their intentions
Teaching is chiefly a way to preserve the audience response to an earlier event
questions.evidence: combine materials rather than assume that one record is sufficient
questions.explanation: Evidence: “combine materials rather than assume that one record is sufficient” Different sources preserve different features of a time-based event.

questions.stem: What can interviews contribute?
options: Explanations of decisions not clear in a recording
A guarantee that memories have not changed
A complete replacement for video
Identical future performances
questions.evidence: explain decisions that are not obvious from a recording
questions.explanation: Evidence: “explain decisions that are not obvious from a recording” Interviews supply interpretation but require critical treatment.

questions.stem: Why might archivists teach a performance practice?
options: Some practical skills are difficult to transmit through recordings alone
Teaching prevents any variation
Written notation includes every gesture
Future participants need no historical context
questions.evidence: skills that a recording alone cannot transmit fully
questions.explanation: Evidence: “skills that a recording alone cannot transmit fully” Living instruction can preserve abilities beyond the recorded sound.

questions.stem: What does “Such accounts” refer to?
options: The explanations given in interviews
Paintings kept in an archive
Every written programme
The audience’s recorded applause
questions.evidence: interviews can explain decisions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “interviews can explain decisions” The caution about memory applies to interview accounts.

questions.stem: Why contrast a painting with a performance?
options: To introduce the difference between an enduring object and an event
To rank visual art above music
To argue that paintings change more rapidly
To propose replacing concerts with exhibitions
questions.evidence: a performance unfolds through actions in time
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a performance unfolds through actions in time” The contrast explains why preservation methods must differ.

items.title: Finding order in a collection
items.passage:
A museum collection can be arranged in several ways. Objects might be grouped by the place they came from, the material used to make them, or the activity they supported. Each arrangement highlights some relationships while making others less visible. A room of metal objects, for example, allows comparison of techniques across regions but may separate tools from the communities that used them.
Digital catalogues can give an object several descriptive tags, allowing users to explore more than one arrangement. This flexibility does not remove the need for judgment. A tag reflects a decision about what feature matters, and older descriptions may use categories that a community now contests. Revising the catalogue can require consultation as well as technical editing.
Visitors also bring different questions. Someone studying manufacture may want material classifications, while someone tracing family history may look for geographic connections. Providing several routes into the collection can serve both. No display is neutral simply because it is orderly; organization is part of the interpretation presented to the public.

questions.stem: What is the central point about organizing museum objects?
options: Organization shapes interpretation and can support different questions
Material classifications provide the most useful interpretation for museum visitors
Digital tags resolve the limitations of older catalogues by increasing technical flexibility
Geographic arrangements should replace other classifications to restore community context
questions.evidence: organization is part of the interpretation
questions.explanation: Evidence: “organization is part of the interpretation” Classification emphasizes selected relationships rather than remaining neutral.

questions.stem: What can material grouping make easier?
options: Comparing techniques across regions
Keeping all objects from one community together
Removing contested descriptions automatically
Tracing every visitor’s family history
questions.evidence: comparison of techniques across regions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “comparison of techniques across regions” The metal-object example identifies a benefit alongside a cultural-context cost.

questions.stem: Why might revising a catalogue require consultation?
options: People may disagree with inherited categories
Tags cannot be changed technically
Objects lose their material properties
Every visitor uses the same research question
questions.evidence: categories that a community now contests
questions.explanation: Evidence: “categories that a community now contests” Classification involves social judgment as well as data entry.

questions.stem: What does “contests” mean in paragraph 2?
options: Challenges
Organizes into a competition
Records carefully
Adopts without question
questions.evidence: a community now contests
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a community now contests” The community disputes the categories rather than participating in a contest.

questions.stem: Why describe two visitors with different interests?
options: To show why multiple ways of exploring are useful
To prove geography is more useful than manufacture
To require every visitor to trace family history
To reject digital catalogues
questions.evidence: Providing several routes into the collection can serve both
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Providing several routes into the collection can serve both” Different interests justify more than one organizational path.

items.title: Reading a tree ring
items.passage:
In many temperate trees, growth produces a visible ring each year. The width and composition of rings can contain information about conditions experienced by the tree. A narrow ring might reflect dry weather, but it could also result from competition, disease, or damage. Interpreting it requires more than matching width to a single cause.
Researchers strengthen an interpretation by comparing several trees from the same area. If many show unusually limited growth at the same time, a shared environmental influence becomes more plausible. A pattern found in only one tree may have a more local explanation. Even a shared pattern must be checked against what is known about the species and the site.
Old wooden objects can sometimes preserve long records, but their history introduces complications. Timber may have been stored or reused before construction. The date represented by its final ring therefore need not be the date of the building in which it was found. Ring evidence becomes more informative when combined with records of construction and careful examination of the wood.

questions.stem: What does the passage emphasize?
options: Tree-ring evidence is valuable but must be interpreted with context
Regional ring patterns directly identify the weather responsible for growth changes
The final growth ring offers a practical date for the construction of a wooden building
Comparing tree species is chiefly useful for choosing timber suitable for reuse
questions.evidence: Interpreting it requires more than matching width to a single cause
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Interpreting it requires more than matching width to a single cause” Multiple influences and timber histories limit simple readings.

questions.stem: Which condition besides dryness can narrow a ring?
options: Competition
Later reuse of the timber
The date of a building record
The number of researchers
questions.evidence: competition, disease, or damage
questions.explanation: Evidence: “competition, disease, or damage” These are listed influences on tree growth.

questions.stem: Why compare trees from one area?
options: A common pattern may indicate a shared environmental influence
Every tree must have the same ring width
It eliminates the need to consider species
It proves that the timber was never stored
questions.evidence: a shared environmental influence becomes more plausible
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a shared environmental influence becomes more plausible” Comparison separates possible shared effects from individual disturbances.

questions.stem: Which statement best restates the point about the final ring and building date?
options: The wood may predate the building because it was stored or reused
A building is always older than the wood used in it
The final ring dates the first time the building was repaired
Stored wood stops containing growth information
questions.evidence: Timber may have been stored or reused before construction
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Timber may have been stored or reused before construction” The paraphrase preserves the reason why ring date and construction date may differ.

questions.stem: Why mention disease and damage?
options: To show that narrow rings have alternative explanations
To suggest that ring studies should use only damaged trees
To explain why all trees form rings
To date the construction of wooden objects
questions.evidence: it could also result from competition, disease, or damage
questions.explanation: Evidence: “it could also result from competition, disease, or damage” The alternatives caution against attributing every narrow ring to weather.

items.title: The timing of a decision
items.passage:
People deciding whether to replace a household appliance may compare purchase prices while overlooking later running costs. A cheaper machine can use more electricity, making it more expensive over its lifetime. However, future savings do not help a household that cannot afford the larger initial payment. A decision that appears inefficient from a long-term perspective may reflect an immediate financial constraint.
Information can change the comparison but does not remove every barrier. Labels that estimate annual energy use make costs easier to compare. Yet actual expenses depend on how often the appliance runs and on future energy prices. Estimates are useful guides rather than promises of an exact saving.
Policies designed to encourage efficient purchases can address both information and access. A payment arrangement may help with the initial cost, while clear labels support comparison. Evaluating such a policy requires asking who can use it, not simply whether the efficient model is available. Availability in a shop and practical affordability are different conditions.

questions.stem: What is the passage’s main point?
options: Long-term value must be considered alongside information and immediate affordability
Clear energy labels are sufficient to make efficient appliances accessible to households
Lifetime running costs should determine a purchase regardless of the initial payment
Payment arrangements matter primarily because they improve the precision of energy estimates
questions.evidence: Availability in a shop and practical affordability are different conditions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Availability in a shop and practical affordability are different conditions” The passage distinguishes lifetime efficiency from practical access.

questions.stem: What affects actual running expenses?
options: Usage frequency and future energy prices
Only the initial purchase price
The number of models on display
The size of a label
questions.evidence: how often the appliance runs and on future energy prices
questions.explanation: Evidence: “how often the appliance runs and on future energy prices” The label is an estimate because these factors can vary.

questions.stem: Why might someone choose a less efficient machine?
options: The more efficient one requires an unaffordable initial payment
They have been guaranteed lower lifetime costs
Energy use is identical for every household
The shop has no information labels
questions.evidence: cannot afford the larger initial payment
questions.explanation: Evidence: “cannot afford the larger initial payment” An immediate constraint can explain a choice despite future savings.

questions.stem: What does “constraint” mean here?
options: A limiting condition
An exact prediction
A preferred design
A future refund
questions.evidence: an immediate financial constraint
questions.explanation: Evidence: “an immediate financial constraint” The phrase describes a limit on what the household can pay now.

questions.stem: Why distinguish availability from affordability?
options: To show that policy evaluation must consider whether people can use an option
To recommend removing efficient machines from shops
To show labels are unnecessary
To prove that all payment arrangements fail
questions.evidence: asking who can use it
questions.explanation: Evidence: “asking who can use it” An option’s presence alone does not establish access.

items.title: A boundary between habitats
items.passage:
The edge between a forest and an open field is not merely a line on a map. Light, wind, and temperature can differ near the edge from conditions deeper inside the forest. These changes affect which plants grow and which animals can find suitable shelter. Some species benefit from the mixture of habitats, while others depend on interior conditions.
When a large forest is divided into smaller patches, its total area may decline only modestly while the proportion exposed to edges increases substantially. Measuring area alone can therefore miss an important ecological change. Two patches of equal area can also have different amounts of edge if one is compact and the other long and narrow.
Conservation planning consequently considers shape and surrounding land use as well as size. A buffer of vegetation may soften some changes at a boundary, but it will not reproduce every feature of an undisturbed interior. The usefulness of a measure depends on which species and processes it is meant to protect.

questions.stem: What should forest conservation consider besides area?
options: The amount and conditions of habitat edges
Compact forest patches benefit conservation mainly by reducing the amount of land required
Vegetated buffers can substitute for the conditions of a forest interior
Forest area is a sufficient planning measure when neighbouring patches have equal size
questions.evidence: shape and surrounding land use as well as size
questions.explanation: Evidence: “shape and surrounding land use as well as size” Edges create conditions not captured by area alone.

questions.stem: Which patch can have more edge for the same area?
options: A long narrow patch
A compact patch in every case
One measured on a newer map
One with no surrounding land use
questions.evidence: one is compact and the other long and narrow
questions.explanation: Evidence: “one is compact and the other long and narrow” Shape changes perimeter relative to area.

questions.stem: Why may modest area loss still matter greatly?
options: Fragmentation can expose more of the remaining forest to edge conditions
Every interior species prefers bright light
The remaining patches stop containing trees
Buffers remove all boundary effects
questions.evidence: the proportion exposed to edges increases substantially
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the proportion exposed to edges increases substantially” The ecological effect can exceed what total area loss suggests.

questions.stem: What does “These changes” in the first paragraph refer to?
options: Differences in light, wind, and temperature
Only the loss of forest on a map
Animal movement between continents
The addition of conservation buffers
questions.evidence: Light, wind, and temperature can differ near the edge
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Light, wind, and temperature can differ near the edge” The phrase points to the environmental differences just listed.

questions.stem: Why qualify the benefit of a vegetation buffer?
options: To explain that it cannot fully recreate interior conditions
To show that buffers always worsen edge effects
To eliminate species-specific planning
To argue that forest shape is irrelevant
questions.evidence: will not reproduce every feature of an undisturbed interior
questions.explanation: Evidence: “will not reproduce every feature of an undisturbed interior” The qualification prevents treating a buffer as a complete substitute.

items.title: How standards coordinate work
items.passage:
A standard can allow products made by different organizations to work together. If a connector has a common size and arrangement, users need not obtain every component from the same supplier. This can support competition and simplify replacement. Agreement is valuable because the usefulness of one product may depend on compatibility with many others.
Establishing a standard also involves choices. A design suitable for existing equipment may not be ideal for future devices. Changing it can improve performance but impose costs on people who already own incompatible products. Keeping it indefinitely may protect those investments while limiting new possibilities.
Standards bodies therefore need procedures for evaluating proposals and managing transitions. An announced change can include a period during which both versions are supported. Clear identification helps users distinguish them. The technical specification matters, but so does how the change is communicated and adopted. Coordination depends on participants knowing which rules apply and when, rather than simply on publishing a document.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The benefits and transition challenges of shared standards
Shared standards mainly benefit users by preventing changes to existing designs
A published technical specification is sufficient to coordinate a transition
Competition among suppliers depends chiefly on replacing common connectors with proprietary designs
questions.evidence: evaluating proposals and managing transitions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “evaluating proposals and managing transitions” Standards enable compatibility but changes require deliberate coordination.

questions.stem: How can a common connector benefit users?
options: It permits components from different suppliers to work together
It prevents replacement of damaged parts
It requires purchase from one manufacturer
It eliminates all future design choices
questions.evidence: users need not obtain every component from the same supplier
questions.explanation: Evidence: “users need not obtain every component from the same supplier” Compatibility reduces reliance on a single source.

questions.stem: Why might organizations support two versions temporarily?
options: To ease the move from existing equipment to a new standard
To hide which rules apply
To prevent any performance improvement
To make both versions permanently indistinguishable
questions.evidence: a period during which both versions are supported
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a period during which both versions are supported” A transition period reduces disruption while adoption occurs.

questions.stem: What does “impose” mean in the second paragraph?
options: Create or require people to bear
Measure precisely
Pay on someone’s behalf
Avoid completely
questions.evidence: impose costs on people
questions.explanation: Evidence: “impose costs on people” A change can place a financial burden on existing owners.

questions.stem: Why mention communication alongside specification?
options: Successful coordination requires users to understand adoption rules
The technical design is always unimportant
Participants cannot read documents
All changes must be delayed indefinitely
questions.evidence: knowing which rules apply and when
questions.explanation: Evidence: “knowing which rules apply and when” Implementation depends on shared understanding as well as the written design.

items.title: Waiting and perceived service
items.passage:
Waiting time has a measurable duration, but people do not judge service solely by counting minutes. Uncertainty can make a wait feel longer. A passenger who knows when the next bus is expected can plan differently from one who sees no information, even if both eventually wait the same amount of time.
Progress information can help, provided it is credible. An estimate that changes without explanation may increase frustration rather than reduce it. Giving a precise time is not always better than giving a realistic range, especially when conditions are variable. Explaining a delay can also distinguish an unavoidable disruption from an impression that staff are ignoring users.
This does not mean information substitutes for improving service. A display cannot create a bus that has not arrived. Instead, operational improvements and communication address different aspects of the experience. Evaluating a change may therefore require both actual timing data and reports of how confidently users could make decisions during the wait.

questions.stem: What is the author’s main point?
options: Credible information affects waiting experience but does not replace better service
Accurate displays improve service mainly by shortening the physical waiting period
Providing a precise estimate is preferable to explaining the uncertainty of a delay
Passenger reports should replace actual timing data when evaluating a service change
questions.evidence: operational improvements and communication address different aspects
questions.explanation: Evidence: “operational improvements and communication address different aspects” The author distinguishes physical service performance from perceived uncertainty.

questions.stem: What can increase frustration?
options: An estimate that changes without explanation
A realistic range under variable conditions
An explanation of an unavoidable delay
Information that lets passengers plan
questions.evidence: An estimate that changes without explanation
questions.explanation: Evidence: “An estimate that changes without explanation” Credibility matters; information is not automatically beneficial.

questions.stem: When might a range be preferable to one precise time?
options: When arrival conditions vary
When no passengers are waiting
When the bus has already arrived
When staff want to conceal all uncertainty
questions.evidence: especially when conditions are variable
questions.explanation: Evidence: “especially when conditions are variable” A realistic range can communicate uncertain conditions better than false precision.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the point of the last paragraph?
options: Improving service and informing users solve related but different problems
A display is enough to improve the operation of every bus
Timing data should replace passenger feedback
Communication matters only when service cannot improve
questions.evidence: operational improvements and communication address different aspects
questions.explanation: Evidence: “operational improvements and communication address different aspects” The paraphrase preserves the distinction without dismissing either approach.

questions.stem: Why use two passengers with the same wait?
options: To isolate the effect of information from the duration itself
To show that both always feel equally frustrated
To compare bus fares
To argue that uncertain schedules attract passengers
questions.evidence: even if both eventually wait the same amount of time
questions.explanation: Evidence: “even if both eventually wait the same amount of time” Holding duration constant illustrates how information changes experience.

items.title: A migrating bird’s compass
items.passage:
Some migrating birds travel at night, when familiar landmarks are difficult to see. Experiments suggest that they can use the pattern of stars as a directional reference. This does not mean that a bird memorizes every star. The rotation of the sky around a relatively stable point can provide information about direction.
Young birds raised beneath an artificial sky offer a way to investigate this ability. When the apparent centre of rotation is changed during their early experience, their later orientation can change too. Such findings suggest that learning contributes to the stellar compass rather than the entire system being fixed at birth.
Birds also respond to magnetic information and other environmental cues. A cloudy night therefore need not make navigation impossible. Different cues can help under different conditions, and disagreement between them can require adjustment. Researchers distinguish a compass, which indicates direction, from a map, which provides information about location. Knowing which way is north alone does not tell a bird how far it is from its destination.

questions.stem: What does “orientation” mean in the artificial-sky experiment?
options: The direction a bird faces or travels
The location where a bird was born
The length of a migration route
The brightness of the visible stars
questions.evidence: their later orientation can change too
questions.explanation: Evidence: “their later orientation can change too” The altered rotation changes directional behaviour, not birthplace, distance, or brightness.

questions.stem: Which feature of the night sky can provide directional information?
options: Its rotation around a relatively stable point
The brightness of each individual star
The distance between the bird and a star
The appearance of familiar ground landmarks
questions.evidence: The rotation of the sky around a relatively stable point
questions.explanation: Evidence: “The rotation of the sky around a relatively stable point” The passage identifies a pattern of movement rather than individual brightness or distance.

questions.stem: Why describe birds raised under an artificial sky?
options: To explain evidence that experience shapes a stellar compass
To explain why natural stars change their rotation
To demonstrate how researchers measure flight distance
To identify the magnetic cue used on cloudy nights
questions.evidence: learning contributes to the stellar compass
questions.explanation: Evidence: “learning contributes to the stellar compass” Changing early experience produces a later directional change; the experiment concerns learning.

questions.stem: What could a bird still lack if its compass works correctly?
options: Information about its present location
A consistent indication of direction
An ability to face north
A reference for comparing directions
questions.evidence: a map, which provides information about location
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a map, which provides information about location” A compass supplies direction; it does not itself locate the bird.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Bird navigation combines learned directional references with multiple kinds of information
Bird migration is chiefly a process of recognizing individual stars
Artificial skies replace the magnetic information used during migration
A working compass provides both the direction and distance to a destination
questions.evidence: Different cues can help under different conditions
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Different cues can help under different conditions” The passage combines stellar learning, other cues, and the distinct roles of compass and map.

items.title: Water climbing through small spaces
items.passage:
Water placed in a narrow glass tube can rise above the surface of the surrounding liquid. Attraction between water and glass helps pull the liquid upward, while cohesion holds neighbouring water molecules together. The curved surface of the water reflects the balance of these forces. This movement through a narrow space is called capillary action.
The width of the space matters. In a narrower tube, the upward force acts along a larger boundary relative to the amount of water being lifted. Water can consequently rise farther than it does in a wider tube of the same material. The rise stops when the upward effect is balanced by the weight of the water.
Paper towels contain networks of small spaces between fibres. Water moving into those spaces allows a towel to absorb a spill. The process does not require a pump, but neither does it mean that water can climb without limit. The material, the liquid, and the dimensions of the spaces all influence the result. Capillary action explains many familiar movements of water that occur without an externally powered device.

questions.stem: What eventually limits the rise of water in a glass tube?
options: The weight of the lifted water
The disappearance of attraction to glass
A change in the tube’s diameter during use
The separation of all neighbouring molecules
questions.evidence: balanced by the weight of the water
questions.explanation: Evidence: “balanced by the weight of the water” The upward effect remains present but is balanced by the downward weight.

questions.stem: What does “cohesion” refer to in this passage?
options: Attraction holding water molecules together
Attraction between water and the glass
The width of an empty tube
The weight of a paper towel
questions.evidence: cohesion holds neighbouring water molecules together
questions.explanation: Evidence: “cohesion holds neighbouring water molecules together” The passage distinguishes molecule-to-molecule cohesion from attraction to another material.

questions.stem: Which comparison would best isolate the effect of tube width?
options: Two glass tubes of different widths in the same water
A glass tube and a paper towel in different liquids
Two tubes of different materials and different widths
A narrow tube before and after its water evaporates
questions.evidence: a wider tube of the same material
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a wider tube of the same material” Keeping material and liquid constant permits a comparison focused on width.

questions.stem: Why discuss a paper towel?
options: To connect the described mechanism to a familiar application
To show that fibres absorb water through a separate powered mechanism
To establish that towels contain straight glass tubes
To compare the weight of glass with the weight of paper
questions.evidence: small spaces between fibres
questions.explanation: Evidence: “small spaces between fibres” The example applies capillary movement to a network of narrow spaces.

questions.stem: Which factor affecting capillary movement is NOT identified?
options: The age of the surrounding container
The material forming the spaces
The liquid involved
The dimensions of the spaces
questions.evidence: The material, the liquid, and the dimensions of the spaces
questions.explanation: Evidence: “The material, the liquid, and the dimensions of the spaces” The final paragraph identifies these three factors, but does not discuss container age.

items.title: The clock inside a mineral
items.passage:
Some minerals contain radioactive elements that gradually change into other elements. The original element is called the parent, and the product of its decay is called the daughter. Because decay occurs at a predictable rate, the relative amounts can help researchers estimate when a mineral formed.
This mineral clock depends on what happened after formation. If heat or fluid allows parent or daughter atoms to enter or leave, the measured ratio may no longer represent undisturbed decay. Researchers therefore examine whether a sample remained a closed system. They may compare different minerals in a rock or use more than one radioactive system to investigate a suspicious result.
A mineral’s age must also be related carefully to the question about the rock. A sedimentary rock can contain grains that formed long before they were transported and deposited together. Dating one such grain does not directly establish when the sediment became a rock. Radioactive decay supplies a physical clock, but geological interpretation determines which event that clock can meaningfully date.

questions.stem: What does “its decay” in the first paragraph refer to?
options: The transformation of the parent element
The formation of the daughter mineral
The transport of a sediment grain
The movement of fluid into a rock
questions.evidence: the product of its decay
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the product of its decay” The daughter element results from radioactive change in the original parent element.

questions.stem: Why might a grain’s age exceed the age of the sedimentary rock containing it?
options: The grain formed before it was transported and deposited
Decay began only after the sediment became rock
The rock lost its grains during heating
Sedimentary deposits contain only daughter elements
questions.evidence: grains that formed long before they were transported
questions.explanation: Evidence: “grains that formed long before they were transported” Grain formation and later deposition are separate events.

questions.stem: What could disturb a mineral’s radioactive clock?
options: Movement of parent or daughter atoms into or out of it
Predictable decay in a closed system
Comparison with another mineral from the rock
Recognition of the mineral’s original formation event
questions.evidence: allows parent or daughter atoms to enter or leave
questions.explanation: Evidence: “allows parent or daughter atoms to enter or leave” Exchange changes the measured ratio; comparison is a way to investigate the disturbance.

questions.stem: What qualification does the passage place on radioactive dating?
options: A reliable age requires both an appropriate sample history and interpretation of the dated event
A predictable decay rate is sufficient to date the deposition of any rock
Different radioactive systems measure only the movement of geological fluids
Daughter elements become useful only after sedimentary grains are deposited
questions.evidence: which event that clock can meaningfully date
questions.explanation: Evidence: “which event that clock can meaningfully date” The passage explains the physical mechanism, possible disturbance, and the distinction between mineral and rock events.

questions.stem: Why might researchers compare different radioactive systems?
options: To investigate whether a result reflects a disturbed sample
To make radioactive elements decay at the same rate
To convert sedimentary grains into a closed system
To determine the route by which grains were transported
questions.evidence: use more than one radioactive system to investigate a suspicious result
questions.explanation: Evidence: “use more than one radioactive system to investigate a suspicious result” An independent comparison can test the interpretation; it does not alter decay or restore the sample.

items.title: Why a coral loses its colour
items.passage:
Many reef-building corals contain tiny algae within their tissues. The algae use sunlight to produce energy-rich compounds, some of which support the coral. The coral provides the algae with a protected environment and access to substances they need. This association helps explain why many reefs develop in shallow, well-lit water.
Under stressful conditions, including unusually warm water, the association can break down. Corals may lose the algae or the pigments associated with them. Their pale skeletons then become visible through the tissue, creating the appearance known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but it has lost an important source of nutrition.
If favourable conditions return soon enough, algae can become established again and the coral may recover. Prolonged stress makes recovery less likely. The outcome depends on the duration and severity of the disturbance as well as the condition of the coral. Bleaching is therefore a visible sign of a disrupted relationship, rather than a simple colour change with no effect on the organism’s energy supply.

questions.stem: What does the passage explain about coral bleaching?
options: It reflects disruption of an association that supplies corals with nutrition
It is the ordinary replacement of a coral’s skeleton during growth
It indicates that a coral has already recovered from warm water
It occurs when corals gain a larger number of algae
questions.evidence: a visible sign of a disrupted relationship
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a visible sign of a disrupted relationship” The passage connects colour, the coral-alga association, nutritional loss, and possible recovery.

questions.stem: What does “established” mean in the recovery discussion?
options: Living and functioning within the coral again
Classified as a new species by researchers
Exposed beneath the coral’s tissue
Transported permanently into deeper water
questions.evidence: algae can become established again
questions.explanation: Evidence: “algae can become established again” Here establishment means re-forming the association inside the coral.

questions.stem: What makes a bleached coral appear pale?
options: Its skeleton becomes visible through the tissue
Its algae produce additional pale compounds
Its tissue develops a thicker protective coating
Its skeleton moves to the outside of the organism
questions.evidence: Their pale skeletons then become visible through the tissue
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Their pale skeletons then become visible through the tissue” Loss of algae or pigment exposes the appearance of the underlying skeleton.

questions.stem: Why could bleaching reduce a coral’s ability to sustain itself?
options: It removes access to compounds supplied by the algae
It prevents the coral from providing shelter to other reef animals
It increases the amount of sunlight reaching every alga
It replaces the coral’s skeleton with algal tissue
questions.evidence: lost an important source of nutrition
questions.explanation: Evidence: “lost an important source of nutrition” The energy-rich compounds from algae are a nutritional resource that is reduced when the relationship breaks down.

questions.stem: Why state that a bleached coral is not necessarily dead?
options: To distinguish a potentially reversible disruption from death
To suggest that prolonged stress improves recovery
To explain why bleaching has no nutritional consequences
To identify colour as the cause of unusually warm water
questions.evidence: the coral may recover
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the coral may recover” The later recovery discussion supports the distinction, while duration and severity still matter.

items.topic: Why a coral loses its colour

items.title: Goods travelling by many hands
items.passage:
Long-distance trade across Eurasia often involved a series of exchanges rather than one merchant travelling the entire route. Goods could move from a producer to a local trader, then pass through several markets before reaching a distant buyer. The journey of an object could therefore be much longer than the journey of any person who handled it.
This arrangement allowed traders to use local knowledge. Someone familiar with one region’s languages, roads, and trading customs could operate there without mastering conditions everywhere else. At meeting points, merchants exchanged goods with others who knew the next region. Transport costs and the risks of each stage contributed to the price paid at the final destination.
Goods were not the only things that travelled. Techniques and stories could spread through contact at markets, although their forms might change as different communities adopted them. Archaeologists finding an imported object can infer contact across regions, but the object alone does not prove that its maker visited the place where it was found. Exchange networks connected distant societies through many shorter movements.

questions.stem: What can an imported object establish without proving a visit by its maker?
options: Contact between regions through exchange
The complete itinerary of one merchant
The absence of any intermediate markets
The language spoken by its final buyer
questions.evidence: does not prove that its maker visited
questions.explanation: Evidence: “does not prove that its maker visited” An object can travel through several people, so its location supports exchange rather than a particular person’s journey.

questions.stem: How did traders benefit from handling only part of a route?
options: They could rely on knowledge of the region where they operated
They avoided paying any transport costs
They supplied goods directly to every distant buyer
They no longer needed to understand local customs
questions.evidence: allowed traders to use local knowledge
questions.explanation: Evidence: “allowed traders to use local knowledge” Regional expertise is the stated benefit; costs and additional exchanges remain.

questions.stem: What does “their forms” in the last paragraph refer to?
options: The techniques and stories being transmitted
The roads through each trading region
The merchants’ written price lists
The imported objects’ makers
questions.evidence: Techniques and stories could spread
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Techniques and stories could spread” The phrase concerns cultural material changing as communities adopt it.

questions.stem: Why contrast an object’s journey with a person’s journey?
options: To introduce exchange through successive intermediaries
To calculate the speed of a particular caravan
To show that producers received the final sale price
To describe a route followed by every merchant
questions.evidence: a series of exchanges rather than one merchant
questions.explanation: Evidence: “a series of exchanges rather than one merchant” The contrast explains how goods can cover a long distance without one person travelling all of it.

questions.stem: Which statement best restates the passage’s point about prices?
options: Costs and risks accumulated along the route affected the final price
Final buyers paid only the production cost because each stage was local
The final price determined which languages regional traders learned
All transport stages involved the same costs and risks
questions.evidence: Transport costs and the risks of each stage contributed to the price
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Transport costs and the risks of each stage contributed to the price” The paraphrase keeps the cumulative contribution without inventing equal costs or a reversed cause.

items.title: Two ways a molten rock cools
items.passage:
Molten rock can solidify beneath the ground or after reaching the surface. Below ground, surrounding rock provides insulation, and cooling is often slow. Crystals have more time to grow before the material becomes solid. At the surface, heat can escape more quickly, commonly producing smaller crystals.
The relationship between cooling and texture helps geologists interpret a rock’s history. A rock with large crystals embedded in a fine-grained background can record two stages. Crystals may begin growing during slow cooling below ground, followed by more rapid cooling after the remaining melt moves upward. The final texture preserves evidence of both stages rather than requiring all crystals to have formed together.
Texture is informative, but chemical composition also matters. Different minerals crystallize under different conditions, and the same general cooling process can produce rocks with different compositions. Geologists therefore examine mineral identity alongside crystal size. A visible texture offers clues to the rate and sequence of cooling; it does not by itself specify every feature of the molten material’s origin.

questions.stem: Why can crystals grow larger during cooling below ground?
options: Insulation allows more time before solidification
The surrounding rock supplies already finished crystals
All minerals form at a single low temperature
The melt loses heat faster beneath the surface
questions.evidence: Crystals have more time to grow
questions.explanation: Evidence: “Crystals have more time to grow” The passage links insulated, slow cooling to growth time.

questions.stem: What could large crystals in a fine-grained background indicate?
options: Slow initial cooling followed by faster cooling
A single period of equally rapid cooling throughout
The mixing of sediment with an already solid rock
Faster cooling followed by identical crystal growth everywhere
questions.evidence: can record two stages
questions.explanation: Evidence: “can record two stages” The passage explicitly connects the two textures to different parts of the cooling history.

questions.stem: What does “embedded” mean in the texture description?
options: Set within the surrounding material
Removed from the molten material
Larger than the entire rock sample
Chemically identical to the background
questions.evidence: large crystals embedded in a fine-grained background
questions.explanation: Evidence: “large crystals embedded in a fine-grained background” The word describes location within material, not chemical identity or removal.

questions.stem: Which information is NOT described as a clue geologists examine?
options: The distance from the sample to a modern road
The size of crystals
The identity of minerals
The presence of a fine-grained background
questions.evidence: mineral identity alongside crystal size
questions.explanation: Evidence: “mineral identity alongside crystal size” Texture and minerals are discussed; modern road distance is not.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the passage?
options: To explain how cooling history influences rock texture and how that evidence is interpreted
To classify rocks solely by the temperature of the surface
To show that large crystals occur only in rocks that never move upward
To explain why different minerals must have identical chemical compositions
questions.evidence: rate and sequence of cooling
questions.explanation: Evidence: “rate and sequence of cooling” The passage explains both texture formation and its use alongside compositional evidence.

items.topic: Two ways a molten rock cools

items.title: A partnership beneath the soil
items.passage:
Many plants form associations with fungi living around or within their roots. The fungi extend fine threads into the surrounding soil, reaching spaces that roots alone may not explore effectively. Through this network, a plant can gain access to water and nutrients, while the fungus receives carbon-containing compounds produced by the plant.
The exchange is influenced by the environment. When nutrients are scarce, additional access can make the fungal association especially valuable to a plant. Where those nutrients are readily available, the benefit may be smaller relative to the carbon the plant supplies. Describing the association as a partnership does not mean that its costs and benefits are identical in every setting.
Researchers investigate these exchanges by following labelled substances through plants and fungi. They can compare nutrient movement under different soil conditions rather than infer the exchange merely from the presence of fungal threads. Such experiments help distinguish the physical extent of a network from what it actually transfers. The association links organisms with different abilities, but its practical effect depends on the resources available to each.

questions.stem: Why follow labelled substances through plants and fungi?
options: To measure what is transferred rather than only observe the network
To increase the number of fungal threads in every soil
To replace the carbon compounds supplied by the plant
To show that root systems do not absorb any water
questions.evidence: what it actually transfers
questions.explanation: Evidence: “what it actually transfers” Following substances tests exchange; the visible presence of threads alone does not establish movement.

questions.stem: What does the plant provide to the fungus?
options: Carbon-containing compounds
Fine threads extending through the soil
Labelled minerals from an experiment
A supply of already absorbed fungal roots
questions.evidence: carbon-containing compounds produced by the plant
questions.explanation: Evidence: “carbon-containing compounds produced by the plant” The plant provides these compounds, while the fungus extends the soil network.

questions.stem: Why might a plant benefit less when nutrients are abundant?
options: Additional nutrient access may be less valuable relative to its carbon cost
The fungus necessarily stops growing any threads
The plant can no longer produce carbon compounds
Water must then be absent from the soil
questions.evidence: the benefit may be smaller relative to the carbon
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the benefit may be smaller relative to the carbon” Resource availability changes the balance; the passage does not claim that growth or carbon production stops.

questions.stem: What does “scarce” mean in the second paragraph?
options: Available only in limited amounts
Distributed equally through all soils
Transferred in a labelled form
Stored exclusively in plant roots
questions.evidence: When nutrients are scarce
questions.explanation: Evidence: “When nutrients are scarce” The contrast is with nutrients being readily available.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: Plant-fungus exchange joins complementary abilities, with benefits that depend on soil conditions
Fungal networks give every plant an equal supply of nutrients
The size of a fungal network directly proves the amount it transfers
Plants receive carbon from fungi in exchange for soil water
questions.evidence: depends on the resources available to each
questions.explanation: Evidence: “depends on the resources available to each” The passage describes the direction of exchange, variable benefits, and experimental evidence.

items.title: Reusing the letters on a printed page
items.passage:
Movable-type printing uses separate pieces bearing raised characters. A printer arranges them to form lines, applies ink, and presses paper against the surface. After printing, the pieces can be separated and used to compose another page. Unlike a block carved for one complete page, the same stock of letters can support many different arrangements.
Reuse creates practical requirements. A workshop needs enough copies of frequently occurring letters, and the pieces must be kept in an order that lets workers find them efficiently. A shortage of one letter can delay composition even when many other pieces are available. Distributing the type back into its storage compartments is therefore part of production, not merely tidying up afterward.
Producing repeated copies does not eliminate errors. A misplaced character may appear in every impression until the arrangement is corrected. A printer who notices it during a run can change the type, leaving earlier and later copies with different readings. Historians comparing those copies can sometimes identify a correction made during production. The reusable mechanism supports repetition while also permitting changes within a single printing run.

questions.stem: What does the passage explain about movable type?
options: Reusable characters permit varied composition but require organization and correction
A separately carved block is required for every arrangement of reusable letters
Reusing type makes all copies of a page identical regardless of corrections
Storage compartments determine the meaning of the printed text
questions.evidence: supports repetition while also permitting changes
questions.explanation: Evidence: “supports repetition while also permitting changes” The passage covers reuse, workshop organization, and correction during a run.

questions.stem: Why might a workshop have much type yet be unable to compose a page promptly?
options: It lacks enough pieces for a particular frequent letter
Its paper has already received ink
Its storage compartments contain different characters
It has printed a page with a different arrangement before
questions.evidence: A shortage of one letter can delay composition
questions.explanation: Evidence: “A shortage of one letter can delay composition” Total stock is insufficient if the required mix of letters is unavailable.

questions.stem: What happens to the type after a page has been printed?
options: It can be separated and arranged for another page
It must remain fixed as a complete page block
Its characters are erased before every new impression
It is replaced by the inked paper
questions.evidence: pieces can be separated and used to compose another page
questions.explanation: Evidence: “pieces can be separated and used to compose another page” The reusable pieces distinguish movable type from a whole-page carved block.

questions.stem: Why compare earlier and later copies from one run?
options: To identify a correction made while printing was underway
To establish which workshop owned the most type
To determine how much ink each character absorbed
To prove that all readers noticed the original error
questions.evidence: identify a correction made during production
questions.explanation: Evidence: “identify a correction made during production” Different readings can preserve evidence of a change to the type arrangement.

questions.stem: What does “it” in “notices it during a run” refer to?
options: A misplaced character
The entire stock of letters
A storage compartment
The carved page block
questions.evidence: A misplaced character may appear in every impression
questions.explanation: Evidence: “A misplaced character may appear in every impression” The printer notices the error just introduced and corrects the arrangement.

items.topic: Reusing the letters on a printed page

items.title: Clues in an animal track
items.passage:
A footprint can identify more than the presence of an animal. Its position relative to other prints may suggest direction and gait, while its depth can reflect both the animal's weight and the softness of the ground. The same animal can leave different-looking tracks on wet soil, sand, or a firm surface.
Interpreting a trail therefore requires comparing clues rather than treating one mark as decisive. A deep print does not necessarily indicate a heavier animal if the ground beneath it was softer. Overlapping tracks may also come from different times. Rain or wind can alter older marks, making them harder to compare with recent ones.
Trackers can record surface conditions and measure several prints along a trail. Photographs with a scale preserve size information, but a picture may not show the ground's resistance when the print was made. Combining the visible pattern with knowledge of the substrate supports a more cautious interpretation. The aim is to identify the explanation best supported by the available traces, while keeping alternatives in view.

questions.stem: What approach to tracks does the author recommend?
options: Interpret several clues in relation to ground conditions
The depth of one footprint provides the most direct estimate of an animal’s weight
Photographs are sufficient to reconstruct the ground’s resistance when a track formed
Track direction is determined mainly by the age of the oldest visible footprint
questions.evidence: comparing clues rather than treating one mark as decisive
questions.explanation: Evidence: “comparing clues rather than treating one mark as decisive” The argument emphasizes contextual interpretation.

questions.stem: What can relative print positions suggest?
options: Direction and gait
The exact time of rainfall
The animal’s diet
The observer’s distance from the trail
questions.evidence: may suggest direction and gait
questions.explanation: Evidence: “may suggest direction and gait” Arrangement is evidence about movement, not the other listed features.

questions.stem: Why might two prints from one animal have different depths?
options: The ground can vary in softness
The animal must belong to two species
The photographs must use different scales
The prints must have been made in different years
questions.evidence: both the animal's weight and the softness of the ground
questions.explanation: Evidence: “both the animal's weight and the softness of the ground” Depth has more than one cause, so varying substrate can explain variation.

questions.stem: What does “substrate” mean here?
options: The surface material beneath the animal
The sequence of photographs
The age of an overlapping print
The animal’s pattern of movement
questions.evidence: wet soil, sand, or a firm surface
questions.explanation: Evidence: “wet soil, sand, or a firm surface” The later term refers to the material on which tracks form.

questions.stem: Why mention what a photograph cannot show?
options: To identify a limitation of visual records
To reject photographs with scales
To prove all tracks disappear quickly
To prefer weight estimates over gait
questions.evidence: may not show the ground's resistance
questions.explanation: Evidence: “may not show the ground's resistance” The limitation explains why contextual evidence complements images.

items.title: Making a public map
items.passage:
A public map simplifies space so that users can find what they need. A transit map may enlarge the city centre and straighten a route, even though these changes distort geographic distances. Such choices can make interchanges clearer. The map is successful if it helps with the intended journey, not if every feature is drawn at the same scale.
Simplification also creates risks. A traveller may assume two nearby-looking stations are within a short walk when the diagram does not preserve distance. Clear labels and an explanation of scale can reduce this misunderstanding. A separate geographic map may be needed for walking.
Accessibility adds further design requirements. Distinguishing routes only by colour can make them difficult for some users to identify. Combining colour with names, symbols, or line patterns provides more than one cue. A useful map therefore depends on both the information selected and the ways that information is communicated. Testing it with actual users can expose confusions that seem invisible to its designer.

questions.stem: What makes a simplified public map useful?
options: Design choices that match user tasks and communicate clearly
A consistent geographic scale is the main requirement for every transit diagram
Colour differences provide the clearest route information without additional labels
Straightened routes are chiefly intended to help travellers estimate walking distances
questions.evidence: the information selected and the ways that information is communicated
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the information selected and the ways that information is communicated” Purpose, clarity, and accessibility guide the design.

questions.stem: Why may a transit map straighten routes?
options: To clarify connections and interchanges
To shorten the actual train journey
To make every station walkable
To remove the need for route labels
questions.evidence: make interchanges clearer
questions.explanation: Evidence: “make interchanges clearer” Diagrammatic changes aid reading without changing the transport system.

questions.stem: Why might a walking traveller need another map?
options: The transit diagram may distort distances
The transit map contains no stations
Every route name is unreliable
Colour prevents all geographic representation
questions.evidence: the diagram does not preserve distance
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the diagram does not preserve distance” Walking requires geographic information that a schematic may omit.

questions.stem: What does “Such choices” in paragraph 1 refer to?
options: Enlarging the centre and straightening routes
Testing users and adding symbols
Taking a shorter walk between stations
Naming the city’s districts
questions.evidence: enlarge the city centre and straighten a route
questions.explanation: Evidence: “enlarge the city centre and straighten a route” The phrase points back to the stated simplifications.

questions.stem: Why recommend combining colour with other cues?
options: To support users who cannot easily distinguish colours
To make all routes share a name
To avoid testing the design
To restore exact geographic distances
questions.evidence: difficult for some users to identify
questions.explanation: Evidence: “difficult for some users to identify” Redundant visual cues improve identification without requiring colour alone.

items.title: Restoring a damaged text
items.passage:
An old manuscript may survive with missing words, faded ink, or torn pages. Editors preparing a readable version sometimes propose restorations using the remaining letters and the author's usual language. A plausible restoration is an interpretation, however, rather than a newly discovered piece of the original.
Other copies can provide evidence, but they are not automatically independent. Two manuscripts may share an error because one was copied from the other or both came from the same earlier copy. Counting identical readings without considering this relationship can exaggerate their support. Editors examine patterns of differences to understand how versions may be connected.
A careful edition distinguishes visible text from supplied wording and explains uncertain decisions in notes. This lets readers assess the evidence instead of receiving a smooth text that conceals its gaps. An edition designed for general reading may present fewer notes than a scholarly one, but it should still avoid implying certainty where the source does not provide it. Readability and transparency need to be balanced rather than treated as identical goals.

questions.stem: What does careful textual restoration require?
options: Separating interpretation from surviving evidence
Agreement among copies provides sufficient evidence for restoring any missing wording
Producing a smooth readable text is the main test of a restoration’s accuracy
Scholarly editions should select a single reconstruction rather than disclose uncertain decisions
questions.evidence: distinguishes visible text from supplied wording
questions.explanation: Evidence: “distinguishes visible text from supplied wording” The passage emphasizes transparent decisions and uncertain evidence.

questions.stem: How can two copies share an error?
options: They may derive from a common earlier copy
They must be independent witnesses
They were always written by the original author
They contain no readable letters
questions.evidence: both came from the same earlier copy
questions.explanation: Evidence: “both came from the same earlier copy” A shared source can transmit the same error.

questions.stem: Why can counting identical readings exaggerate support?
options: Related copies may repeat one source rather than provide independent evidence
All copied words necessarily differ
More copies always create new facts
Notes make readings impossible to compare
questions.evidence: they are not automatically independent
questions.explanation: Evidence: “they are not automatically independent” Dependence reduces the force of repeated agreement.

questions.stem: What does “supplied” mean in paragraph 3?
options: Added by an editor to fill a gap
Written visibly in the surviving source
Purchased from a manuscript owner
Copied without any uncertainty
questions.evidence: visible text from supplied wording
questions.explanation: Evidence: “visible text from supplied wording” The contrast distinguishes surviving words from proposed restoration.

questions.stem: Why include notes on uncertain decisions?
options: To let readers evaluate the basis for restorations
To prove that the source had no damage
To replace all readable text
To count every copy as independent
questions.evidence: lets readers assess the evidence
questions.explanation: Evidence: “lets readers assess the evidence” Notes expose decisions that a seamless version might conceal.

items.title: The uneven spread of an innovation
items.passage:
A new practice rarely spreads through a community at a uniform rate. Some people try it early, while others wait to observe results. Adoption can depend on cost, available support, and whether the practice fits existing routines. A useful technique may spread slowly if trying it involves substantial risk.
Communication networks affect what people learn. An early adopter who is trusted by neighbours may provide more persuasive evidence than a distant advertisement. Yet a network can also circulate an incomplete account, especially when successful cases receive more attention than failures. Observing apparent popularity does not establish that a practice works equally well for everyone.
Researchers studying diffusion therefore examine both information and circumstances. Two households hearing the same recommendation may make different choices because they have different resources. [A] One might have spare equipment to test a method, whereas another cannot afford a failed trial. [B] These differences help explain why awareness does not always lead to adoption. [C] A sound evaluation asks who can benefit under which conditions. [D] Access to support may matter as much as awareness of the technique.

questions.stem: What explains unequal adoption of a practice?
options: Differences in networks, resources, and fit with routines
A trusted recommendation makes practical resources less important to adoption
The rate of adoption chiefly reflects how effectively advertisements demonstrate success
Apparent popularity provides the strongest evidence that a practice fits different households
questions.evidence: both information and circumstances
questions.explanation: Evidence: “both information and circumstances” Knowledge interacts with practical ability and perceived risk.

questions.stem: Who can provide persuasive evidence in a community?
options: A trusted early adopter
Only a distant advertiser
Only someone who has never tried the practice
Every popular account regardless of accuracy
questions.evidence: An early adopter who is trusted by neighbours
questions.explanation: Evidence: “An early adopter who is trusted by neighbours” Trust in a local user can make their experience persuasive.

questions.stem: Why might two informed households make different decisions?
options: Their capacity to absorb the risk may differ
They must have heard different recommendations
The innovation cannot be useful to either
Awareness guarantees the same response
questions.evidence: cannot afford a failed trial
questions.explanation: Evidence: “cannot afford a failed trial” Resource differences can change what is feasible.

questions.stem: Which labeled sentence gives a concrete example of unequal resources?
options: Sentence A
Sentence B
Sentence C
Sentence D
questions.evidence: One might have spare equipment to test a method
questions.explanation: Evidence: “One might have spare equipment to test a method” A describes the contrast; B explains its implication and C states an evaluation principle.

questions.stem: Why mention the prominence of successful cases?
options: To warn that circulating accounts can be selective
To prove failures never occur
To require everyone to adopt quickly
To show advertisements are always inaccurate
questions.evidence: successful cases receive more attention than failures
questions.explanation: Evidence: “successful cases receive more attention than failures” Selective attention can distort the apparent evidence.

items.topic: The uneven spread of an innovation

items.title: Life on a temporary pond
items.passage:
A temporary pond fills during a wet period and later dries. Its inhabitants must either complete vulnerable life stages while water remains or survive the dry interval in another form. Some organisms produce resistant stages that persist in sediment until suitable conditions return. The absence of visible activity during drought therefore does not necessarily mean the habitat has lost all life.
The duration of water availability can vary greatly between years. A species that succeeds during a long wet season may fail when the pond dries unusually early. Studying one year alone can give a misleading impression of a stable community. Repeated observations reveal how persistence depends on both life history and environmental timing.
Temporary ponds may also contain fewer predators that require permanent water, although this does not make them risk-free. Changing the depth or drainage of a pond can alter its drying pattern and thus its community. Conservation needs to consider the cycle of filling and drying, rather than assume that keeping water present continuously is always an improvement.

questions.stem: What is the central argument about temporary ponds?
options: Their ecological value depends on a cycle that species have adapted to
Maintaining permanent water is the most effective way to protect temporary-pond communities
A successful wet season provides a reliable description of a pond’s long-term community
The absence of visible activity during drought indicates that organisms must recolonize from elsewhere
questions.evidence: the cycle of filling and drying
questions.explanation: Evidence: “the cycle of filling and drying” The pond’s temporary nature shapes survival and conservation needs.

questions.stem: How can some organisms survive a dry period?
options: As resistant stages in sediment
By requiring permanent water predators
By remaining visibly active throughout drought
By preventing all evaporation
questions.evidence: resistant stages that persist in sediment
questions.explanation: Evidence: “resistant stages that persist in sediment” The passage identifies a dormant survival strategy.

questions.stem: Why might one year’s survey be misleading?
options: Water duration and species success vary between years
